story_text.value:
Code has become extremely cheap to produce, if you have a 5x claude subscription, you can produce or at least try to produce any piece of software you want. And, to be honest, I actually like that, I feel more people should build their own tools and release them as open source because everyone gets to turn their ideas into real products, for their own use if not for others.

But this also means it is getting easier to copy a product, put it on public GitHub and announce you've killed the paid version. Being open source shouldn't give you a pass for shipping slop. If you are calling your tool a replacement for something people pay for, show how it compares.

In the past week, each time I opened X, I kept seeing ads about a new open source code review tool claiming to be the "CodeRabbit killer". I have used CodeRabbit in the past and it definitely has its shortcomings, but if you're claiming you've killed a product, there needs to be evidence.

I saw the advertisement so many times that I decided to evaluate how the product actually performs, it also gave me an excuse to add review capabilities into my own open source tool called shadowclone which helps me manage my agent skills and ensure that regardless of the harness or model I use, agents consistently follow my engineering preferences.

I ran an eval using Greptile, OpenQodex (the open source tool I wanted to evaluate), and my own implementation of a code reviewer in shadowclone, which is basically a code review skill, a local reviewer and a Github bot that can review on the cloud.

My bot reported a higher proportion of findings that both model judges considered real, but it missed 4 real bugs that Greptile caught and as for OpenQodex, I will let the results speak for themselves.

1. Greptile found 69% of the known bugs and 68% of its findings were judged as real 2. shadowclone cloud bot found 38% and 96% of the findings were judged as real 3. shadowclone locally found 36% and 91% of the findings were judged as real 4. OpenQodex found 31% and 86% of its findings were judged as real

The local reviewers ran 3 times per PR. You can see the full eval results at https://github.com/theonly1me/shadowclone/tree/main/evals/code-review

The harness is open source too and you can re-run the eval if you like.

I still want more people to build and release their own tools. I am doing it too. But, if you advertise yours as a replacement for an existing product, I want to see what you tested and where it falls short. Mine missed bugs Greptile caught and publishing that gives me something useful to work on, calling it a Greptile killer wouldn't.

story_text.value:
Hey, I'm Akhil, co-founder of Tessary. An open-source agent reliability platform that monitors every production trace, detects issues that sampled evals miss, and investigates to find the root cause.

We started up about a year ago building synthetic users for usability testing of B2B software, we built the agents that would personify real users and use the software but, we were never able to make them work reliably enough for long running sessions. We had built a massive eval set to tune our agents but, then the evaluation itself got prohibitively costly - like 5x costlier than actually running the agent since we needed to grade across the many narrow intents of our agent. That's where Tessary originated, we wanted to make agent reliability both cover more ground and be simultaneously less costly to run.

Tessary works on 2 layers.

L1 classifiers - which look at every agent trace and flag potentially erroneous ones extremely cheaply. We are talking 2-3 orders of magnitude cheaper than running the actual agent.

L2 agents - which triage and find the root cause of the issue from the erroneous traces. These are run on SOTA models but, because we run them on already flagged traces, the time and $ spent finding the cause is much cheaper than running grading on even 1% of traces. In our testing on complex agents, at 1M traces, this approach was 5x cheaper than sampled evaluations and as your agent gets more reliable, the cost of reliability also goes down.

we are open source and can be self-hosted so, you don't need to send your traces to us. We support existing `gen_ai` spec and ingestion over OTLP so, you can add this as a new exporter to your existing setup. We have a cloud version, you can quickly try the features with a $10 credit.

We are looking to build more classifiers and enable people to build custom classifiers for their needs and would love to hear feedback on common failure modes people have built solutions or evaluation for

Repo: https://github.com/tessaryai/tessary Website: https://tessary.ai Try for free: https://app.tessary.ai

story_text.value:
Hi everyone,

When I first heard about WebMCP 6 weeks ago, I started thinking about what problems it might create. One question that came to mind was how developers would evaluate WebMCP tools and monitor them in production. That's when I decided to build Senro, a platform that helps devs test WebMCP tools using goal-oriented evals, trajectory evals, and more across LLMs, as well as monitor how those tools are used in production. Senro has a free plan (not a free trial). You can monitor up to 25K events/mo and run up to 250 evals/mo using your own API key (sorry, we're not venture-backed yet).

story_text.value:
As a forward deployed engineer at Meta, I spent the past 2 years working with businesses implementing AI agents.

A few problems: 1) Businesses want control over their AI agents: the code, the tools, the skills, everything. Meta, for obvious reasons would never do that. Nor OpenAI, nor Anthropic. 2) The LLM does everything. But that costs money. There are many routines in an AI agents that don't need an LLM. 3) For an AI agent to solve a real business problem, the business must own the eval data set. Similar to point #1 above, most don't do that.

Instead, I built an opensource AI agent that you can write it all in TypeScript code and own everything, locally. Use any model, talk to it via any channels, set limits on token usage, look at the logs and adjust. All of this in one small npm package.

At this point, I would like to get feedback if these is a gap in the market for something like this. It's supposed to be simple and get you started. It doesn't solve ALL problems related to deploying AI agents. It's in version 0.25.1 right now.

Have a look: https://chloejs.org/compare

story_text.value:
I'm obsessed with Egyptology. During covid, I wanted to get a hieratic tattoo. For those who don't know, hieratic is the cursive form of hieroglyphs that was used in day-to-day life in ancient Egypt. It's as old as hieroglyphs.

I then went on a mission to have a sentence translated into hieratic. Luckily, in 2022, I was able to commission an Oxford Egyptologist to write it for me. After that, I took it to a hieratic specialist I found on Instagram to redraw it with "biblical" accuracy.

When generative AI came out, I realized that models very rarely identify hieratic and almost never translate it correctly. Every single time a new model came out, I ended up testing my sentence and hieratic texts in general, and I realized this could actually become a benchmark. Since so many benchmarks are becoming saturated, we need to find weird ways to test new models.

That's why I decided to build HieraticBench.

The first version of the benchmark has 268 items, including real documents, signs, and other Egyptian scripts, which I used as controls, as well as my unpublished sentence in two different renditions. The current state-of-the-art foundation models are hilariously bad at identifying my sentence, especially the one the Egyptologist wrote with her pen. Some of them said Tibetan, Urdu, Korean, and, funnily enough, "Reformed Egyptian," which is from the Book of Mormon.

On real documents, the best model in the benchmark identified hieratic correctly 95% of the time, and the best score for reading individual signs was around 13%. That's when we tell the model specifically that it's hieratic. None of them can really translate a sealed sentence that's never been published and has no answer key.

I haven't run every model on every task just to keep costs down. My next steps were to run Astra and Gemini 3.1 Pro on real documents. Currently, only the Claude models have done the sign readings.

And just FYI, I have no experience whatsoever running benchmarks or evaluations, so not 100% sure I scored things right.

Things we need: - Running the models I haven't covered - More sealed sentences and labeled signs

If you know hieratic or have an Egyptologist friend, reach out at hieraticbench@veeza.ai.

Source code: https://github.com/alymoursy/hieraticbench

I'll be around to answer questions.

story_text.value:
This is actually a reincarnation of a project I did almost 10 years ago (GitSpo). I index social sites (X, Bluesky, Reddit, HackerNews, etc) and track content that mentions any GitHub repository. If you are an open-source author – this gives you a daily or weekly summary of all social mentions of your project. If you are evaluating open-source projects, this allows you to validate them by observing that has been said about these projects in public forums.

Provided as a public service. Doesn't cost you anything.

story_text.value:
Hi HN, we built TOD, a model and API for jevlike LLM pipelines.

we have people using it for, routing a ticket, classifying intent, deciding whether something is urgent, or rating severity.

Architecture - 12B Gemma fine-tuned to score options. since it is gemma based it has multimodality built in - When there are >120 labels, we have a 150M retriever that narrows them to a shortlist (recall@16 is 0.9–1.0 on our evals), and the 12B model scores that shortlist. - Context goes up to 49k tokens, with up to 8 images per request.

we have open sourced it,

model: https://huggingface.co/parsecai/tod API: https://parseclab.ai/tod

We are working on getting the RL environments to finetune for custom use cases.

would love to hear your opinions on this.

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I was frustrated with expiring credits, subscriptions and generally BS approach in image&video generation space (which is now universally useful and basically a commodity) so I've built Azurade, a hosted service where you have 35+ models (Veo3.1, Seedance 2.5, Wan 3.0, Nano Banana, GPT Image2.5 etc.) behind one non-expiring, fully agent native balance. I care about billing, that's why credits are prepaid and never expire, a failed generation is refunded automatically, and you can buy a pack without a subscription. I got tired of monthly credits (or usage) that vanish at the end of the month

This post is mainly about it's remote MCP server, because that's how I and my friends mostly use it now (via Claude or Codex)

You can add https://azurade.com/mcp in Claude or Codex (or claude code), sign in once through OAuth and the LLM will be able to generate / get all info about models and account / upload files and all that.

I've ran it through oblivious evaluator agent for 8 times to reach good agent ergonomics. After all, if I want to build an agent-native service the users (agent) should evaluate and correct it. Please feel free to point your agents at it and send me the nitpicks and gotchas they encounter. Humans are also welcome :)

Demo video (1m40s, cute dog included): https://youtu.be/tX29WLffXCk

P.S. the stack is Go and Pocketbase, official GO MCP SDK, and the frontend is statically rendered NextJS. The access token is an API key named after the client, so revoking an agent means deleting that key on your profile page. It also works like REST API with an OpenAPI spec.
